extracted.intended_audience: appellate counsel and parties in patent IPR appeals (Federal Circuit / patent litigators)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evidentiary criteria for establishing Article III standing to appeal a Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB) final written decision to a federal court, as applied in Federal Circuit precedent. Focuses on what constitutes a concrete injury in fact based on threatened or potential patent infringement and the proof required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article III standing elements
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish a case or controversy under Article III, the appellant must meet the irreducible constitutional minimum of standing: (1) suffered an injury in fact, (2) that is fairly traceable to the challenged conduct of the defendant, and (3) that is likely to be redressed by a favorable judicial decision. (Spokeo v. Robins; Lujan.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the three-part Spokeo/Lujan test. Injury must be 'concrete and particularized' and 'actual or imminent, not conjectural or hypothetical.' Cite Spokeo, 578 U.S. at 338–39; Lujan, 504 U.S. at 560. Apply traceability and redressability to connect the alleged harm to the Board's decision and to show relief from a favorable ruling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injury-in-fact must be concrete, particularized, and imminent
rubrics_metrics.description: An injury in fact must be 'concrete and particularized' and 'actual or imminent, not conjectural or hypothetical.' (Spokeo.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegations of speculative or hypothetical harm are insufficient. Show specific, imminent harm (e.g., identified products, customers, contracts, dates, or steps likely to produce infringement). Generalized fear of suit or abstract business harms do not satisfy this requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing required for judicial review of agency final action (but not to appear before agency)
rubrics_metrics.description: A party does not need Article III standing to appear before an administrative agency, but standing is required once the party seeks review of an agency’s final action in a federal court. (Cuozzo; Phigenix.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between administrative participation (no Article III standing requirement) and seeking federal-court review (Article III standing required). When appealing a PTAB final written decision to the Federal Circuit, demonstrate Article III standing independently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for standing
rubrics_metrics.description: The party seeking judicial review bears the burden of proving standing. (JTEKT Corp.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The appellant must present admissible evidence and specific factual assertions sufficient to establish each element of standing. Conclusory assertions are insufficient; submit declarations, documentary evidence, or other concrete proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: When relying on potential infringement liability, show concrete plans creating substantial risk of suit
rubrics_metrics.description: If a party relies on potential infringement liability as the basis for standing, it 'must establish that it has concrete plans for future activity that creates a substantial risk of future infringement or [will] likely cause the patentee to assert a claim of infringement.' (JTEKT Corp.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide detailed plans for future conduct (specific products, customers, timelines, design/material choices) and explain why those plans create a substantial risk of infringement or would likely provoke suit. Vague development plans or generalized business intent do not suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speculation or generalized threats are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere speculation about the possibility of suit or generalized statements about a patentee’s proclivity to sue are insufficient to confer standing. (Apple v. Qualcomm; Prasco.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying solely on patentee’s prior litigation history or broad warning letters. Show particularized evidence connecting the patentee’s asserted patents to specific products or conduct at issue now or imminently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dismissal with prejudice undermines inference of future suit
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior infringement suits dismissed with prejudice weigh against finding a substantial risk of future litigation based on the same claims. (Apple cited; case facts noting dismissal with prejudice.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If relevant claims were dismissed with prejudice in prior actions between the parties, explain why current circumstances nevertheless create a substantial risk of renewed suit (e.g., new products materially different, newly asserted claims, or changed legal posture).

rubrics_metrics.name: Declarations must identify specific product particulars and plans
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits or declarations supporting standing must provide non-conclusory, detailed information: concrete plans, product specifics (materials, properties), customers, timelines, and how those products may implicate the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclusions like 'we are developing new models' without details (material composition, refractive indices, features) are inadequate. Courts reject vague, conclusory testimony as insufficient to show concrete plans or substantial risk. (Allgenesis; this decision.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee correspondence must be specific and timely
rubrics_metrics.description: Correspondence from the patentee (e.g., warning letters) can support standing only if the communication is specific to the threatened activity and reasonably connected in time and content to the asserted risk of suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A pre-litigation broad warning letter sent before intervening events (such as subsequent dismissals with prejudice) or lacking specificity about the accused products or models is weak evidence. Show that the patentee's statements are targeted to the present concrete plans or products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petitioner need not concede infringement to establish standing
rubrics_metrics.description: IPR petitioners need not concede infringement to establish standing to appeal. (JTEKT Corp. cited.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While petitioners may deny infringement, they still must present concrete, non-speculative facts showing that their planned or ongoing activity creates a substantial risk of suit or injury. The absence of a concession does not relieve the evidentiary burden on standing.
